title_original: Caleb Stein: A Truce Runs Through It
excerpt_original: Photographer Caleb Stein found a no-trespassing swimming hole in the Hudson Valley where Americans who have nothing in common meet for an afternoon in the water. L’article Caleb Stein: A Truce Runs Through It est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: Caleb Stein arrives in Poughkeepsie in 2013 to study at Vassar College, a private university in this former industrial city. Steeped in the Norman Rockwell imagery of a childhood split between London and New York, he picks up his camera to put those inherited myths to the test of lived experience. His partner and closest collaborator, artist and photographer Andrea Orejarena, shows him the way: a dirt path through the trees, a few No Trespassing signs, and beyond them, a sandbank cradled in a bend of Wappinger Creek — a pool twenty-one meters by nine, the size of a tennis court, where locals and passersby find each other. “I’ve been an open-water swimmer since childhood,” he tells Blind at Oddity gallery, which showed “Down by the Hudson” during Paris Photo. “But this place was, first and foremost, somewhere we came to rest.”

Water has always been credited with the power to transform. Caleb Stein is its witness. What first catches his eye is a strange ritual: men wade into this stretch of river fully dressed, shoes and all. “They come in with this armor,” he says, “wanting to create distance between the outside world and themselves. But the water clings so tightly to the skin that it makes them vulnerable anyway.” More suggestive than nakedness, that second, soaking skin opens a breach: the bravado dissolves, shoulders drop, and the swimmer surrenders to an enchantment of the senses. In the milky black-and-white prints, the sensuality of bodies surfaces with the taste of an eternal summer — all ages, all classes, indistinct.

The marvelous sits right up against the mundane: a drive-in on one side, an American Legion hall on the other — one of those rooms where veterans gather around a bar and a flag. On the sandbank, Vassar students brush past families up from the Bronx for the day, relatives visiting from Jamaica, kids from Poughkeepsie whom Caleb Stein himself taught to swim. “You see people at risk of being deported by ICE swinging off the same rope as die-hard Trump supporters. It’s a little like Christmas Day in World War One — the soldiers stop shooting, walk out into no man’s land, and play a game of football.” The armistice lasts an afternoon. Then everyone climbs back to the bank.

Another paradox in the land of trespassing : authority stops at the waterline. American law allows anyone to stand in the river; the path down to it belongs to the government. So at the sight of a patrol, swimmers drop their sandwiches, leap from their blankets, and throw themselves into the water — blameless citizens again in a single second. “There aren’t that many spaces where people can gather without being closely monitored,” the photographer observes. Shopping malls, parks, sidewalks: everywhere else, surveillance. Here, each person reclaims the land by surrendering to nature rather than subduing it, and the joy of that freedom shows on every face. On the rope you reach by a ladder of planks nailed to the trunks, even the smallest jump draws a crowd. “Maybe democracy begins there,” Caleb Stein tells writer Daniel Wolff in the book, “in the act of looking together.”

Every winter, when the place empties and freezes, Caleb Stein comes back alone — to see which trees have shifted and whether the ladder still holds. Waiting for summer’s return, its gift of recovered innocence: the season when every swimmer becomes a neighbor, an acquaintance, a friend.
Down by the Hudson (first edition) is published by Palo Gallery .
